items.title: 21.5.1 Comparison of Reactivities of Halogenoalkanes and Halogenoarenes

source_refs.note: Topic 21.5.1 with Quick Check 21.4 and the DDT box (PDF 84-85); the delocalisation sketch is redrawn and a comparison table of chloroethane and chlorobenzene is added for the learning outcome. The exercises (PDF 85-87) are not part of the lesson body. Answers need review.

blocks.text: In halogenoalkanes the halogen is attached to an alkyl group. Because carbon and the halogen differ in electronegativity, the carbon attached to the halogen carries a partial positive charge and is electrophilic: nucleophiles attack it, giving a large family of nucleophilic substitution reactions, while bases attacking the neighbouring hydrogen give elimination reactions.

In halogenoarenes, however, a lone pair on the chlorine atom is delocalised into the aromatic ring. This gives the carbon-chlorine bond partial double-bond character, making it stronger and harder to break. As a result halogenoarenes are much less reactive and synthetically less useful than halogenoalkanes; for example, chloroethane is hydrolysed by aqueous sodium hydroxide but chlorobenzene is not under normal conditions.

blocks.title: Interesting information: DDT
blocks.text: Some halogen compounds, such as DDT, have been used as pesticides, but because they persist in the environment their use has been restricted or banned in developed countries. DDT is cheap and effective against mosquitoes, and some developing countries saw malaria deaths rise sharply after it was withdrawn. It is therefore advised to restrict its use to protect the environment.
